capital: Sucre (constitutional capital); La Paz is the seat of government
summary: Bolivia lies in the interior of central South America, with the Andean Altiplano, Lake Titicaca and the Uyuni salt flat, and has one of the highest proportions of indigenous people in South America.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism arrived with the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire in the 1530s; after the discovery of the Potosí silver mine in 1545, Spain established large-scale colonial rule there, and the Catholic Church was closely bound to the colonial regime. Missionaries promoted Catholicism in indigenous communities, but many indigenous people combined Catholic saints with traditional beliefs such as Pachamama, the Earth Mother; for example, the Virgin of Copacabana blends in ancient beliefs of the Lake Titicaca area. The new constitution of 2009 abolished Catholicism's status as the state religion and declared the state secular.

ranking.name: Protestantism / Evangelicalism
ranking.description: Protestantism and Evangelicalism were introduced in the 20th century by American and European missionaries, and since the 1960s have grown rapidly among indigenous people and the urban poor, especially the Pentecostals. They attract followers through community mutual aid, abstinence from alcohol and faith healing, and many Aymara and Quechua people have converted to Evangelicalism, raising its share to nearly 20%.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population in Bolivia is very small, about 6%, concentrated among the young generation and the highly educated in large cities such as Santa Cruz and La Paz. Because religion and indigenous traditional beliefs remain very important in Bolivian society, relatively few people identify as non-religious.

religion.background: Before the arrival of the Spanish, the indigenous peoples of the Andes worshipped the sun god Inti, the Earth Mother Pachamama and the mountain spirits apus, and the Tiwanaku culture on the shore of Lake Titicaca (about 500–1000) was an important religious center. After the Spanish conquest in the 16th century, Catholicism became the official religion of the colony, but indigenous people blended their traditional beliefs into Catholicism, forming a distinctive religious culture. After independence in the 19th century Catholicism remained the state religion, until in 2009 the Morales government promulgated a new constitution establishing the state as secular and respecting indigenous beliefs. In recent years Evangelicalism has grown rapidly and the proportion of Catholics has gradually declined.

language.official: Spanish and 36 indigenous languages are all official languages.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish arrived with Spanish colonization in the 16th century; in the colonial period it was the language of administration and the Church, and it became the national language after independence in 1825. From the mid-20th century, the 1952 revolution promoted land reform and universal education, large numbers of indigenous people moved from the countryside to cities, and the use of Spanish expanded rapidly; today about 70% of the population use it as their main language.

ranking.name: Quechua
ranking.description: Quechua was the official language of the Inca Empire and spread to the highlands and valleys of present-day Bolivia during the Inca expansion of the 15th century. In the colonial period Spanish missionaries also preached in Quechua, which spread it further. Today it is found mainly in departments such as Cochabamba, Potosí and Chuquisaca, and the 2009 constitution lists it, together with other indigenous languages, as an official language.

ranking.name: Aymara
ranking.description: Aymara has a longer history than the Inca Empire and is generally thought to be linked to the ancient civilizations on the shore of Lake Titicaca; it is still concentrated in La Paz Department and around Lake Titicaca. After Evo Morales, the first indigenous president and an Aymara, took office in 2006, the status of Aymara and indigenous culture rose greatly.

ranking.name: Guaraní
ranking.description: Guaraní is found mainly in the Chaco region of the southeast, and its speakers are the indigenous Guaraní people. In the late 19th century the Bolivian army came into conflict with the Guaraní, and after the Battle of Kuruyuki in 1892 many Guaraní lost their land. Today it is one of the official languages, but it has only about 1% speakers.

language.history: Before the Inca Empire, Bolivia already had many languages such as Aymara, and after the Inca expansion in the 15th century, Quechua became the lingua franca of the highlands. After Spanish colonization in the 16th century, Spanish became the language of the ruling class, but indigenous languages continued to be used in the countryside. Universal education after the 1952 revolution promoted Spanish, and indigenous languages were for a time marginalized. The new constitution of 2009 recognized Spanish and 36 indigenous languages as official languages and required civil servants to speak at least one indigenous language, in order to realize the idea of a 'plurinational state'.

ranking.name: Salteña
ranking.description: A baked half-moon pastry whose crust encloses juicy beef or chicken, potatoes, peas, olives and boiled egg, with a slightly sweet and slightly spicy flavor.
ranking.history: The name salteña comes from Juana Manuela Gorriti in the 19th century, a political exile from Salta Province in Argentina, who is said to have made this pastry in Bolivia for a living, so people called it 'the one made by the woman from Salta' (salteña). It shares an origin with the empanada brought by Spain, but the Bolivian version has a filling with a lot of broth. Bolivians habitually eat it as a snack around 10 a.m., and it is regarded as the national snack.

ranking.name: Silpancho
ranking.description: Beef is pounded into a very thin large slice, breaded and fried, and laid over rice and potatoes, then topped with a fried egg and tomato-onion salsa.
ranking.history: Silpancho is the signature dish of Cochabamba, and its name comes from the Quechua word 'silpa' (thin), referring to the beef being pounded very thin. The Cochabamba Valley was already an important agricultural region in the colonial period, known as the 'breadbasket of Bolivia', abundant in rice, potatoes and corn. The dish developed in Cochabamba in the 20th century and has now become a common home-cooked dish across the country.

ranking.name: Pique macho
ranking.description: Chunks of beef, sausage and french fries are piled onto a large plate and topped with onion, tomato, chili peppers and boiled egg, in a huge portion suited to sharing among many people.
ranking.history: Pique macho is also a famous dish of Cochabamba; the 'macho' in the name means 'tough guy', hinting at its portion size and spiciness. There are different accounts of its origin, a common one being that a restaurant in Cochabamba in the late 20th century improvised the dish for hungry late-night customers. It is a popular dish to go with beer when friends get together, and also represents Bolivia's love of hearty meals.

ranking.name: Anticucho
ranking.description: Beef heart is cut into pieces, marinated in chili, cumin and vinegar, skewered and grilled over charcoal, often served with potatoes and peanut chili sauce, a night-time street snack.
ranking.history: The origin of anticucho is linked to slaves and indigenous people of the colonial period: the Spanish masters ate the good cuts of beef and left offal and other lesser cuts to their servants, who marinated and grilled them with spices. The dish is popular across the Andean countries, and the name comes from Quechua. In Bolivia it is a popular snack of evening street vendors, most commonly seen in the night markets of La Paz and Cochabamba.

ranking.name: Sopa de maní (peanut soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup made by simmering raw peanuts ground into powder with beef bone broth, potatoes, macaroni and vegetables, with a rich texture and a nutty fragrance.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and are generally thought to have been first domesticated in the area of present-day Bolivia and northern Argentina; the Incas and even earlier Andean peoples already ate peanuts. Peanut soup combines the indigenous peanut with the beef and wheat pasta brought by the Spanish, an example of post-colonial fusion cuisine. It is especially popular in Cochabamba and Sucre, and is regarded as one of the most representative soups of Bolivia.
